items.text: WTI and Brent crude both surged last week (+1.5% and +2.8%, respectively), settling at $86.48 and $95.29. Underlying tensions related to Middle East conflict and supply tightness continue to drive prices, which feeds into inflation expectations (Michigan consumer survey now shows 4.3% year-ahead inflation vs. 4.2% prior month). For credit investors, higher energy costs pressure refinancing ability in leveraged sectors and increase default risk among energy-sensitive borrowers.

The July payroll collapse (-23K, vs. +20K prior month) starkly contradicts the strong ISM Manufacturing PMI at 55.6 (7th consecutive month expansion). Labor data deterioration is broad: unemployment holding at 4.1%, claims 206K, and AHE growth cooling to 3.15%. This divergence creates uncertainty for the Fed—manufacturing strength suggests demand resilience, but labor weakness hints at softening ahead. For special situations investors, this backdrop raises refinancing risk for highly leveraged or cyclical borrowers facing tighter credit conditions.

Core PCE rose 0.2% m/m and 3.3% YoY in July, in line with expectations and providing the Fed some room to hold rates. Headline CPI eased from 3.5% to 3.4% YoY with core inflation slowing from 2.6% to 2.5%, yet inflation expectations remain sticky at 4.3%, particularly among lower-income and older consumers. Sticky core inflation and elevated medium-term expectations limit the Fed's cutting capacity, keeping terminal rates elevated and extending refinancing pain.

Fed funds locked at 3.75% with modest curve steepening (2s10s now 47 bps vs. 46 bps). Long-dated Treasury yields remained elevated even as short-dated yields declined on softer data, with real yields on 30-year TIPS moving above 3% during recent weeks—a level not seen since 2008. Elevated long-duration real rates and heavy fiscal supply create a structural headwind for long-maturity credit and refinancings, particularly acutely painful for CRE and any bonds maturing beyond 2-3 years.

High-yield OAS tightened modestly to 270 bps (from 275 bps), and investment-grade OAS fell to 81 bps (from 82 bps), signaling resilience; however, CCC OAS widened to 1039 bps (from 1035 bps), hinting at stress in lower-rated issuers. Hyperscaler AI capex issuance accounts for 16–23% of gross IG, HY and leveraged loan issuance YTD, with technology spreads widening partly due to heavy supply, though credit fundamentals appear reasonable for top-of-stack. The bifurcation between prime and distressed credit is acute—special situations investors should focus on stressed and legacy debt where dislocations are largest.

GDP momentum mixed: GDPNow nowcast jumped to 4.61% (a notable revision upward), yet retail sales fell 0.6% in July, their first decline in nine months, missing expectations for a 0.1% gain. Consumer sentiment deteriorated sharply: Michigan sentiment fell ~8% to 51.0 in early August, well below the 55.0 estimate, ending two consecutive months of improvement. The divergence between top-line growth forecasts and consumer weakness suggests a slowdown ahead; credit investors should assume moderating demand and loan growth in 2026.

Retail sales including food services declined 0.6% m/m in July, below expectations for 0.1% gain, with weakness in non-store retail (-2.2% m/m) stemming partly from earlier Amazon Prime Day timing. Housing data continues to weaken: existing home sales at 4.06M (July) and housing starts at 1.239M, both down m/m. 30-year mortgage rates are elevated at 6.65%. The housing market's slowdown and consumer caution signal lower credit demand and higher default risk for consumer-finance and mortgage-backed portfolios.

themeCards.title: CRE Office Distress & Maturity Wall
themeCards.statusLine: Office loan delinquencies in CMBS jumped to record 12.34% in January 2026, the highest level since 2000. Approximately $930 billion of CRE loans mature in 2026, up significantly from 2025, with at least $126 billion distressed; nearly $930 billion CRE loans mature in 2026.
themeCards.relevance: Office represents the largest special situations opportunity in credit markets today. High default and loss severity rates, combined with lender forced sales, create alpha for distressed debt and equity investors who can source, underwrite, and execute restructurings or workouts.

themeCards.title: Consumer Sentiment Cliff & Income Erosion
themeCards.statusLine: Michigan sentiment index fell to 51 in August, down from 55.2 in July and below market expectations of 54.5; both current conditions and expectations components weakened. Only 8% of consumers now expect their incomes to grow faster than inflation, down from 18% in December 2024.
themeCards.relevance: Rapid deterioration in sentiment and income expectations signals near-term risk of credit stress among lower-income borrowers and consumer finance portfolios. Subprime auto, credit cards, and student loan ABS may face higher delinquencies if consumer spending continues to weaken.

themeCards.title: Energy Price Shock & Tariff Inflation
themeCards.statusLine: The August consumer sentiment decline was driven by concerns about inflation linked to Middle East conflict, with the survey conducted while national average gasoline prices remained above $4 per gallon. Energy-linked inflation expectations in Michigan rose to 4.3%.
themeCards.relevance: Energy and tariff-driven inflation creates a stagflationary tail risk that limits Fed easing, extends high rate scenarios, and pressures refinancing ability. Energy-sensitive issuers (transportation, chemicals, industrials) face near-term refinancing headwinds; special situations players should monitor supply-chain constrained sectors for distressed opportunities.

themeCards.title: China Manufacturing Contraction & Demand Weakening
themeCards.statusLine: In July, China's official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.2%, a decline of 1.1 percentage points from the prior month, indicating contraction and a decline in manufacturing climate. Output and new orders contracted, including export orders, while purchasing activity weakened and supplier delivery times lengthened.
themeCards.relevance: Slowing Chinese demand trickles into US corporate earnings (particularly tech, semiconductors, heavy equipment) and could pressure refinancing for export-dependent corporates. Signals a potential global demand slowdown that constrains growth assumptions embedded in credit spreads.

themeCards.title: Long-Duration Real Rates & Fiscal Supply
themeCards.statusLine: Real yields on 30-year inflation-protected Treasuries moved above 3% during recent weeks, reaching the highest level since 2008; heavy government borrowing and elevated bond supply are increasing concern about the availability and cost of long-term capital.
themeCards.relevance: Structural elevation of real rates creates a permanent increase in discount rates for long-dated corporate and real estate debt. This particularly impacts CRE refinancing, leveraged buyout debt, and any bonds maturing beyond 3 years, creating opportunities for distressed holders to force restructurings or sales at deeply discounted valuations.

themeCards.title: Labor Market Divergence & Recession Risk
themeCards.statusLine: July nonfarm payrolls contracted -23K despite ISM Manufacturing PMI at 55.6 (strongest since May 2022), initial claims 206K, and labor force participation weakness. This divergence signals either a pending hard landing or data quality issues; either way, credit markets face elevated uncertainty on default rates.
themeCards.relevance: The payroll collapse creates immediate near-term credit stress for borrowers relying on tight labor assumptions and rising labor costs. A true deterioration in labor demand would cascade into retail, hospitality, and consumer-oriented credit, driving rapid credit spread widening and forcing defensive repositioning.

consensus.GDP: 4.6% GDPNow (current), expectations for 2.0–2.5% annualized in Q3

regime.label: Late-cycle with stagflationary risks
regime.detail: Cooling labor, sticky core inflation, elevated real rates, consumer confidence crumbling, but manufacturing resilient; maturity walls and CRE distress mounting.
